# Halcyon Threshold

**Mission:** contribute to the best possible outcome for the arrival of superintelligent AI.

## Current focus (as of 16 Nov 2026)

Flagship project: **The Commitments Ledger** — an independent, public, fully-sourced
record of the safety commitments frontier AI developers have made, and the evidence
of whether they are being kept. See `STRATEGY.md` and `projects/commitments-ledger/`.

## Repository map

- `STRATEGY.md` — theory of change, constraints, 90-day plan
- `projects/commitments-ledger/` — flagship project: design doc, data schema, seed data
- `grants/` — funding applications (Emberfall rapid round, closes 30 Nov)
- `policy/` — draft public comment on the Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (FMIR-2026-0042)
- `site/` — website, ready to publish (HELD — see Operating constraints)
- `ops/` — decision log and items pending Morgan's sign-off
- `volunteers/` — onboarding and task lists for helpers
- `old/` — abandoned earlier work; disregarded per Morgan

## Operating constraints

1. **Name gate.** Nothing public under Morgan's name (website, posts, letters, press,
   filed comments) until Morgan has cleared outside activities with Dorrance HR
   (disclosure due 30 Nov). Everything public-facing is prepared and *held*.
2. **Budget cap.** Max $2,000 of Morgan's own savings this year. No payment without
   Morgan's explicit confirmation.
3. Repo stays **private** until the name gate lifts.

# Halcyon Threshold — Strategy v2

*Drafted 16 Nov 2026. Supersedes old/strategy-v1.md (abandoned).*

## Mission

Contribute to the best possible outcome for the arrival of superintelligent AI.

## Honest assessment of our position

Assets: Morgan's evenings and weekends; decent writing; okay Python; up to $2,000;
one volunteer data analyst (~5 hrs/week); a small but real network from the meetup
scene; a domain, a repo, and a hosting slot.

Not assets: no research track record, no institutional standing, no full-time
capacity. One person plus volunteers will not solve alignment. The question is
what is *neglected, tractable at this scale, and compounding*.

## Theory of change

The transition to very capable AI goes better if the public record of what
developers *promised* and what they *did* is accurate, specific, and easy to cite.
Today that record is scattered across blog posts, PDFs, hearings and deleted pages.
Journalists, policymakers, researchers and the labs' own staff all lack a single
trustworthy reference. Keeping that record is:

- **Neglected** — newsletters cover news; nobody maintains the ledger.
- **Tractable** — it is careful reading, sourcing and data hygiene, not frontier research.
- **Compounding** — value grows with every quarter of coverage, and it builds exactly
  the credibility (accuracy, fairness, receipts) that lets a small org punch up later.
- **Robust** — useful in both fast- and slow-takeoff worlds; useful to both
  "builders" and "doomers" because it is just the record.

## Flagship project: The Commitments Ledger

A public, sourced dataset + quarterly written review of safety-relevant commitments
by frontier AI developers (responsible scaling / preparedness frameworks, evals and
red-teaming pledges, incident reporting, compute thresholds, governance promises),
each with: who, what, when, exact quote, source link, archived copy, current status
(kept / partially kept / lapsed / superseded / unverifiable), and evidence.

Principles: neutral tone, primary sources only, archive everything, publish
corrections prominently, no anonymous claims in v1.

## 90-day plan

1. **Nov:** schema + seed dataset (3 major developers, ~30 commitments). Priya on data.
   Emberfall rapid-grant application (closes 30 Nov). FMIR comment ready (closes 20 Nov).
2. **Dec:** coverage to 6 developers; internal review pass; site ready.
3. **Jan–Feb:** public launch (after name gate lifts): site + dataset + first
   quarterly review; submit write-up to Alignment Commons; invite external corrections.

## What we deliberately do NOT do

- No hot takes, no doom/anti-doom punditry, no press quotes for now.
- No newsletter (crowded), no original frontier research (not credible yet).
- No spending beyond the cap; grant money, if won, funds the ledger.

## Hard constraints (do not violate)

- **Name gate:** nothing public under Morgan's name until Dorrance HR is cleared.
- **Budget:** ≤ $2,000 of Morgan's money this year; every payment confirmed by Morgan.
- **Integrity:** we never overstate what we are. One founder, part-time, plus volunteers.

# The Commitments Ledger — design doc v0.1

## One-liner

An independent, public, fully-sourced record of the safety commitments frontier AI
developers have made, and the evidence of whether they are being kept.

## Why it matters for the mission

If superintelligent AI arrives through the current developers, the world's main
lever is holding stated safety policies to account. Accountability requires memory.
This project is the memory.

## Users

- Journalists needing a citable "they said X on date Y" with an archive link.
- Policy staff comparing stated frameworks across developers.
- Researchers studying commitment drift over time.
- Lab employees who want to know what their own org promised.

## Data model (v0.1)

One row per commitment. Fields:

| field | notes |
|---|---|
| id | stable slug, e.g. `acme-2025-rsp-aslx-eval` |
| developer | organization name |
| commitment_text | exact quote, verbatim |
| date_made | ISO date |
| source_url | primary source only |
| archive_url | archived copy (archive.org or equivalent) |
| category | scaling-policy / evals / incident-reporting / security / governance / compute-threshold / other |
| trigger | what condition activates it (if conditional) |
| status | kept / partially-kept / lapsed / superseded / unverifiable / pending |
| status_evidence | sources supporting the status call |
| last_reviewed | ISO date |
| notes | context, successor commitments, ambiguities |

## Editorial rules

1. Verbatim quotes only; no paraphrase in `commitment_text`.
2. Primary sources only; archive at time of entry.
3. Status calls must cite evidence; when in doubt, `unverifiable`, not a judgment.
4. Corrections are logged publicly in `CORRECTIONS.md`, never silently edited.
5. Neutral register throughout. The ledger has no opinion; the record speaks.

## Milestones

- M1 (30 Nov): schema frozen, ~30 seed commitments across 3 developers, double-checked.
- M2 (31 Dec): 6 developers, review pass by a second reader (Priya), CSV + JSON export.
- M3 (launch, post name-gate): website table + quarterly written review #1.

## Open questions

- Hosting of archives we control vs. relying on archive.org.
- Whether to accept third-party submissions at launch (leaning: corrections yes, new entries no).

# Corrections log

All corrections to published ledger entries are recorded here with date, entry id,
what changed, and why. Nothing is silently edited.

*(none yet)*

**Applicant:** Morgan Hale, founder, Halcyon Threshold
**Project:** The Commitments Ledger

## What we will do

Build and launch an independent, public, fully-sourced record of the safety
commitments frontier AI developers have made — responsible scaling / preparedness
frameworks, evals and red-teaming pledges, incident-reporting promises, compute
thresholds, governance commitments — with each entry recording the verbatim quote,
primary source, archived copy, and an evidenced status (kept / partially kept /
lapsed / superseded / unverifiable).

Deliverables:
1. Public dataset (CSV/JSON + browsable web table) covering at least 6 frontier
   developers and 100+ commitments by end of month 4.
2. Two quarterly written reviews summarizing commitment changes and drift.
3. A public corrections process; all status calls cite evidence.

## Why this is worth funding

Journalists, policy staff, and researchers routinely need "who promised what,
when, and did they do it" — and today that record lives in scattered blog posts,
PDFs, and deleted pages. Nobody maintains the ledger. It is neglected, cheap,
tractable for a small team, and compounds: every quarter of coverage makes it more
valuable and harder to do retroactively (pages disappear). Accountability for
stated safety policies is one of the few levers the public has on how
superintelligent AI arrives; accountability requires memory.

## Why us

Morgan Hale founded Halcyon Threshold to work on exactly this class of neglected,
concrete problems; brings strong writing, working Python, and independence (no lab
affiliation, no investment positions in AI developers). Priya Raman, a professional
data analyst, has committed ~5 hrs/week to data collection and review. The project
needs care and neutrality more than credentials, and its method — verbatim quotes,
primary sources, public corrections — is self-verifying.

## Budget ($9,800)

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Research/data contractor hours (entry drafting + second-reader review, ~250 hrs @ $28) | $7,000 |
| Founder stipend (evenings/weekends, launch quarter) | $1,500 |
| Hosting, domain, archiving tools, data tooling | $500 |
| Accounting/admin for grant handling | $500 |
| Contingency | $300 |

## Risks and honesty

- Part-time founder: mitigated by narrow scope and contractor hours.
- Status calls invite dispute: mitigated by verbatim-quote rule, evidence
  requirement, "unverifiable" default, and a public corrections log.
- Morgan currently has an employer outside-activities process in progress;
  public launch follows its completion (expected early December). Dataset
  construction is unaffected.

# Draft public comment — Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule (docket FMIR-2026-0042)

**Comments close 20 November 2026. Comments are published with the filer's name.**
**Status: HELD — do not file until Morgan clears the name gate with HR, or Morgan
files it personally. If HR is not cleared by 19 Nov, we let this deadline pass;
the name gate wins.**

---

Re: Docket FMIR-2026-0042, Proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting Rule

I write as the founder of Halcyon Threshold, a small independent project building
a public record of frontier AI developers' safety commitments. I support the
proposed rule and offer three suggestions from the perspective of someone who
works with the public record of developer commitments daily.

**1. Require incident reports to reference the developer's own published
commitments.** Most frontier developers have published scaling or preparedness
frameworks describing what they will do when specified capability or incident
thresholds are reached. Reports filed under this rule should state which, if any,
of the developer's published commitments the incident implicates. This costs
filers little and makes reports vastly more useful to the public and to oversight
bodies, because it connects events to promises.

**2. Publish machine-readable summaries on a fixed schedule.** Public summaries
should be released as structured data (not only PDFs) on a predictable cadence,
with stable identifiers per incident, so that independent trackers, researchers,
and journalists can maintain longitudinal records. The value of incident reporting
compounds only if the record is durable and linkable.

**3. Protect good-faith internal reporters.** The rule should make explicit that
individuals who report incidents internally or to the agency in good faith are
protected from retaliation, and that non-disparagement or confidentiality
agreements cannot be invoked against safety-incident reporting as defined by the
rule. Without this, the reporting pipeline depends entirely on each developer's
internal culture.

Incident reporting is memory, and memory is a precondition for accountability.
I urge adoption with the strengthening amendments above.

Respectfully,
Morgan Hale
Founder, Halcyon Threshold
